source.title: Sparse but not Simpler: A Multi-Level Interpretability Analysis of Vision Transformers

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures neuron-level selectivity, class variance, and label entropy in dense and pruned vision models, and reports that pruning does not meaningfully reduce neuron-level feature multiplexing. This refines the sparsity–interpretability claim, though it does not test the specific 4e:55 example.
record.gate_note: Neuron-level outcomes are described in the text and shown in Fig. 2, but exact values for those metrics are not stated in the text. The paper also reports SAE-feature, circuit, and attribution results; those do not directly measure whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs or whether their polysemanticity changes, so they are not recorded as rows here. The specific mixed-input examples cited in the claim are not investigated.
record.test_reason: The study compares neuron-level polysemanticity proxies (selectivity, class variance, label entropy) between dense and Wanda-pruned DeiT-III B/16. This tests whether one intervention, weight sparsity, changes neuron polysemanticity, which bears on V5 in a new setting (ViT with post-hoc pruning). It is not a replication of the original vision or SoLU work, and it does not argue that a version is wrong, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that weight sparsity via Wanda pruning does not meaningfully reduce neuron-level feature multiplexing, and that neurons and SAE features stay highly polysemantic. They add that sparse models give about 2.5x fewer circuit edges but recruit a larger fraction of nodes ('representation spreading'). Attribution faithfulness improves only modestly at low sparsity. Smaller circuits do not imply semantic interpretability.
record.recipe_differences: Compares dense and Wanda-pruned DeiT-III B/16 models using class-based neuron metrics, rather than reproducing the original circuit study’s individual-neuron feature visualization and causal analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The tested sparsity level changes some outcomes in other analyses, but the paper reports no consistent sparsity-related change in the neuron-level selectivity, entropy, or class-variance results recorded here.

fits_no_version.finding: In dense and pruned DeiT-III B/16, the top attributed MLP neurons show high label entropy over ImageNet classes. Authors read this as neurons being highly polysemantic, but no numeric value is given in the text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons in supervised vision transformers respond broadly across many classes, measured by class-activation entropy. This is a breadth proxy, not unrelated-input polysemanticity.

record.problems: Neuron-level results are shown in a figure without stated numerical values or uncertainty estimates. Polysemanticity is assessed with class-based proxy metrics rather than ground-truth concepts or direct examinations of unrelated stimuli. The study uses one supervised vision-transformer architecture and post-hoc pruning.
record.rows_left_out: None of the neuron-level metrics reported in the text was omitted. SAE feature, circuit, and attribution results were left out because they do not directly measure whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs or whether their polysemanticity changes.

untested.parts: No neuron is shown to respond to specific unrelated inputs. Class-entropy and variance proxies are reported without numbers. InceptionV1 and the cited examples are not studied.
SAE metrics on pruned vs dense models do not test whether more features than neurons causes polysemanticity.

Only post-hoc Wanda pruning plus 2-epoch fine-tuning is tested. Activation functions (SoLU), architectures, sparse-from-scratch training and other regularizers are not tested. Only the top-50 attributed neurons per class are measured, not the share of polysemantic neurons.
Not tested. Only a single set of proxy metrics is used, with no comparison of measurement choices.

missing.what: Numeric neuron-level metric values (entropy, selectivity, CV) per layer and sparsity, including whether a dense distribution is shown

record.verdict_notes: The V1 links were removed from all rows because the class-based proxies (AUROC selectivity, within-class CV, class entropy) cannot show responses to unrelated inputs, and no numbers are reported. The V5 verdict is limits_scope, not challenges: pruning is not among the levers V5 names (activation function, architecture, regularization), and the result shows only that this intervention does not lower the proxies. The SAE results (Fig. 3, Table 2) measure SAE features, not neurons, and are correctly excluded. The ablation-impact metric measures functional concentration, not polysemanticity, and is reasonably omitted. The study is a single-author preprint with one model and no uncertainty reported for the neuron metrics.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test InceptionV1 or neuron 4e:55, and does not inspect the cited cat-face, car-front, and cat-leg inputs. Uses class-based metrics in DeiT-III B/16 rather than direct demonstrations that particular neurons respond to unrelated inputs.
No language models or transformer-language-model MLP neurons are studied.
Does not test whether more sparse features than neurons cause polysemanticity, or directly measure feature-to-neuron capacity pressure.
Does not test polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when there is sufficient capacity for all features.
Tests Wanda pruning followed by fine-tuning, not activation-function changes, alternative architectures, SoLU, or modern convolutional networks.
Does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons with feature visualization or other tools to determine whether their inputs share a feature or job.
Does not compare measurement choices or explanation-scoring methods to determine how they change whether a neuron is classified as polysemantic.

rows.operation_detail: Measured neuron selectivity as AUROC for predicting a target class from the CLS-token activation.

conditions.value: top 50 per category, selected using attribution patching

rows.baseline: Dense model; exact value not stated
rows.value: No consistent change in selectivity across sparsity levels; exact values are figure-only
rows.note: The text reports no consistent selectivity changes across the majority of categories. The study reports the result qualitatively across its tested layers and sparsity levels, not separately as numeric results for each checkpoint.
rows.check: AUROC selectivity measures how well a neuron predicts one class. It measures change across sparsity, not whether a neuron responds to unrelated inputs, so the V1 link is dropped. Neurons are the top-50 per category chosen by attribution patching, not all neurons. The baseline is labelled 'dense', but the 4.2 setup lists only sparsity {0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7}. Whether dense is plotted in Fig. 2 can't be confirmed from the text. Values are figure-only.

rows.note: The text describes class variance as stable across sparsity levels and reports no consistent changes across the majority of categories. This is a proxy for response consistency within a class, not a direct test of unrelated input meanings.
rows.check: Class variance is the within-class coefficient of variation, i.e. response consistency within one class. It cannot show responses to unrelated inputs, so the V1 link is dropped. The text says it is stable across sparsity. The dense-baseline and neuron-selection caveats from R1 apply.

conditions.value: top 50 per category, selected using attribution patching

rows.baseline: Dense model; exact value not stated
rows.value: Entropy remains high and shows no consistent change across sparsity levels; exact values are figure-only
rows.note: The authors interpret high label entropy as evidence that neurons remain similarly polysemantic in sparse and dense models. The class-activation measure is a proxy and does not establish that the classes correspond to unrelated visual inputs.
rows.check: For V5 the relevant fact is that entropy shows no consistent change with sparsity, so the state is absent, not partial. 'Remains high' is a level statement with no number, over class distributions that may include related classes. It does not establish unrelated mixtures, so the V1 link is dropped and the finding moved to fits_no_version. Section 3.2 says averages are over 100 categories, but 4.2 and Fig. 2 say all 1,000. This is an internal inconsistency.

source_check.problem: none; text says label entropy stays high with no consistent change. Sec 3.2 says averages over 100 categories, but Sec 4.2 and Fig. 2 say 1,000.

relationships.condition: Wanda-pruned DeiT-III B/16 at 10-70% weight sparsity with fine-tuning, top-50 attributed neurons, blocks 2/7/11
relationships.reason: Weight pruning, an intervention that keeps accuracy (76.9% vs 83.7% top-1 at 70%), leaves selectivity, class variance and label entropy without consistent change (R1, R2, R3). Not every structural change lowers polysemanticity, though the version's named levers were not tested.
relationships.display_finding: Top-1 accuracy was 76.9% versus 83.7% at 70% sparsity, and selectivity, class variance and label entropy showed no consistent change; the claim's named levers were not tested.

relation.reason: Its own results on neuron-level proxies bear on whether a structural change (weight sparsity) changes polysemanticity (V5).

tranche.reason: New setting (ViT, post-hoc pruning) with its own results on neuron polysemanticity proxies. It does not reproduce the original method (not T1), and the authors do not argue that a version is wrong (not T5).

source_check.notes: All neuron results are figure-only (Fig. 2) and are class-based proxies, which the authors admit. Table 1's text lost the 0.8 column: Wanda top-1 is 0.8044 at 70% and 0.7687 at 80% (dense 0.8371). Sec 3.2 says 100 categories; Sec 4.2/Fig. 2 say 1,000.

statements.correction: Wanda 70%: top-1 0.8044 vs dense 0.8371 (Table 1). Sec 4.1 confirms: 0.18% above magnitude pruning (0.8026), over 96% of dense. 0.7687 is Wanda at 80% sparsity.
statements.problem: Gives Wanda top-1 at 70% sparsity as 76.9%, but that is the 80%-sparsity value. The text extraction lost Table 1's 0.8 column header. The rest of the study-specific part is right: no consistent change in the three measures, blocks 2/7/11, top-50 attributed neurons per class.

Matches: post-hoc Wanda pruning plus two epochs of fine-tuning on supervised DeiT-III B/16; the limitations name sparse-from-scratch training as not studied; class-based proxies on top-50 attributed neurons in blocks 2/7/11.
Listing Wanda pruning as unchanged is right: no consistent change in selectivity, class variance or label entropy.

statements.correction: arXiv:2603.15919: Wanda weight pruning of DeiT-III B/16 (10-70% sparsity, 2-epoch fine-tuning) gave no consistent change in neuron selectivity, class variance or label entropy. It is a structural intervention, not a regularizer.
statements.problem: Lists the study among regularizers that leave the measure unchanged. It tests post-hoc Wanda weight pruning plus fine-tuning, not a regularizer. The authors only speculate that light pruning may act as a mild regularizer, for SAE features and attribution.
